title: The Loop That Only Reacts Is Always Behind: Feedforward

questions.question: A PD loop that settles perfectly on a stationary target is given a target moving at 0.5 m/s. What happens to the error?
options: It settles at a constant value and stays there for as long as the motion lasts
It decays to zero, more slowly than for a step
It grows without bound
It oscillates around zero
questions.explanation: Measured at 0.234 m, constant. A feedback loop is a machine for reacting to being wrong, so following a moving target it must be wrong continuously, because the error is the only thing producing the command.

questions.question: That 0.234 m has two causes. What are they?
options: The plant needing force to move at all, 0.035 m, and the derivative term opposing steady motion, 0.200 m
The proportional gain being too low, and the derivative gain being too high
The plant's inertia and its damping
Sensor lag and actuator lag
questions.explanation: A derivative taken on the measurement contributes minus kd times v during any steady motion, which the proportional term must also overcome from an error. It is the larger of the two here.

questions.question: Feedforward for the plant is added. What does the error become?
options: 0.199 m: exactly the plant's share removed, and the derivative's share untouched
0.001 m: both causes removed
0.035 m: the derivative's share removed
Unchanged, since feedback still dominates
questions.explanation: Each fix removes exactly its own cause and neither removes the other. Taking the derivative on the error instead gives 0.034, and doing both gives 0.001.

questions.question: Why not simply take the derivative on the error, which removes the larger share?
options: A step of setpoint moves the error by the whole step in one sample: measured, 4020 N against 20 N on a one metre step
It is mathematically incorrect
It makes the loop unstable at any gain
It cannot be computed without the setpoint's velocity
questions.explanation: Neither is wrong. They are right about different inputs, and the combination to reach for is feedforward with the derivative left on the measurement.

questions.question: The damping coefficient is unknown. Is feedforward still worth implementing?
options: Yes: leaving that term out entirely was still sixteen times better than no feedforward, and the penalty is proportional and symmetric
No, a wrong model is worse than none
Only if the load is also unknown
Only with an integrator to correct it
questions.explanation: Measured errors of 0.014 with the damping term absent, 0.001 with it right, and 0.016 with it doubled, against 0.234 with no feedforward at all. There is no cliff.

questions.question: Where should the actuator limit be applied?
options: Once, to the total, at the end: clamping the feedback then adding exceeds the limit, and clamping both separately discards authority
To the feedback only, since feedforward is known to be feasible
To each part separately, so both stay in range
Before the feedforward is computed
questions.explanation: A feedforward that reaches the limit on its own is a useful signal rather than a fault: the profile is asking for more than the machine has, before any error has occurred.
